titel: Rental property as an investment in the US
kurz: Four return measures, a fully worked model case and the effect of leverage, which at today's mortgage rates can raise or lower the return on your own money.

bloecke.md:
In economic terms, a rental house resembles a small business more than a savings account. It has revenue, operating costs, a debt ratio and often only one customer. Whether it pays its way has to be shown by a calculation before closing. After that, the all-in cost is fixed, and it is the only variable that can no longer be changed.

Four return measures appear in this calculation. They are often confused, usually to the seller's advantage. The measures differ in which costs are deducted in the numerator and which capital is in the denominator.

bloecke.formel:
Gross rental yield = Annual rent / Purchase price × 100
Price-to-rent ratio = Purchase price / Annual rent
bloecke.erklaerung: The price-to-rent ratio is the reciprocal of the gross rental yield. A ratio of 12.5 corresponds to 8%, a ratio of 20 to only 5%. Neither figure takes costs into account, so both are only suitable as a criterion for sorting listings. The same applies to the "1% rule", which asks for a monthly rent of at least 1% of the price, that is, a gross yield of 12% a year.
bloecke.beispiel: The formula always takes the scheduled rent before vacancy. A listing that shows the rent of a fully let year, or a rent that has not yet been achieved, makes the yield look higher than it will be.

bloecke.md:
The **capitalization rate** (cap rate) and the [[Net rental yield|net rental yield]] correct the numerator. Both start from net operating income (NOI): the rent actually collected after vacancy, minus the costs of running the property, that is, property tax, insurance, maintenance, property management and HOA dues. Mortgage payments and depreciation are not deducted, because they depend on the financing and on taxes, not on the property. The cap rate divides NOI by the price; the net rental yield also adds the closing costs to the denominator.

There are no official rates for the cost assumptions in the US. Common conventions are 5% to 10% of the rent for vacancy, 8% to 10% of the collected rent for professional management and 1% of the price a year for maintenance. Property tax and insurance can be looked up for the specific property. A rough rule of thumb, the "50% rule", says that operating costs take about half of the rent. It is no substitute for a calculation, but it is more realistic than the zero assumption found in many listing calculations.

bloecke.formel:
NOI = Collected rent − Operating costs
Cap rate = NOI / Purchase price × 100
Net rental yield = NOI / (Purchase price + Closing costs) × 100
variablen: property tax, insurance, maintenance, management, HOA dues; not mortgage interest, principal or depreciation
lender and title fees, recording fees, transfer taxes, inspection; typically around 2% to 5% of the price
bloecke.erklaerung: Only the net rental yield can be compared with the return on other investments. However, it does not include financing or changes in value.

bloecke.titel: From price-to-rent ratio to return on equity (illustrative calculation)

bloecke.md: Throughout, the table assumes the same cost burden as the model case below (closing costs 3%, operating costs 47.6% of the scheduled rent), a loan of 75% of the price at an assumed 7.0% and no change in value. In the last column, the current return on equity falls from plus 4.64% to minus 0.04% between a ratio of 8 and a ratio of 10. The ratio rises by a quarter, and the result switches from positive to negative.

## Model case

A single-family house built in 1990 costs $300,000. The rent is $2,000 a month, that is, $24,000 a year. The gross rental yield is 8.0%, the price-to-rent ratio 12.5. Closing costs are assumed at 3%, or $9,000, so the total investment is $309,000. Loans for investment properties usually require a larger down payment, often 15% to 25%, and carry a higher rate than loans for owner-occupied homes. The financing consists of a $225,000 loan, 75% of the price, at an assumed 7.0% over 30 years, with a payment of $1,496.93 a month. The equity of $84,000 covers the closing costs and 25% of the price.

The operating costs are assumed as follows: 5% vacancy, property tax of 1.2% of the price, insurance of $1,800 a year, maintenance of 1% of the price and management at 8% of the collected rent. That leaves net operating income of $12,576, a cap rate of 4.19% and a net rental yield of 4.07%.

bloecke.titel: Annual account for the first year (illustrative calculation, $)
bloecke.unter: After all payments, including principal, $24,000 in rent results in a cash shortfall of around $450 a month before tax and around $230 after the tax effect, provided the loss can be deducted.

bloecke.md:
The tax saving arises because the result on Schedule E is negative. Rental income of $22,800 minus $10,224 in operating costs, $15,678 in mortgage interest and $8,873 in depreciation gives a loss of $11,975. Residential rental buildings are depreciated straight-line over 27.5 years. The basis is the building's share of the purchase price plus the capitalized acquisition costs, here an assumed 80% of $305,000, that is, $244,000; land is never depreciated. In the year of purchase, a mid-month convention reduces the amount slightly; the full-year figure is used here.

Whether the loss reduces taxes depends on the passive activity rules (26 U.S.C. § 469). Rental losses are passive and can normally only be offset against passive income. An exception allows up to $25,000 a year to be deducted from other income for owners who actively participate, for example by approving tenants and setting the rent. This allowance shrinks by 50 cents for every dollar of modified adjusted gross income above $100,000 and disappears at $150,000. At a 22% federal tax rate and with the allowance available, the loss saves $2,634. Above $150,000, it saves nothing for now: the loss is carried forward and can be used against future passive income or when the property is sold.

In the first year, the owner pays in an extra $2,753 after tax, while at the same time $2,285 of principal builds up equity. Overall, wealth thus falls by $468, which is −0.56% on the $84,000 invested, before any change in value. The principal itself is not income. It shifts money from the account into the equity in the house. If you count it as return, your own saving is booked as profit.

variablen: return on the total investment without financing, here net rental yield plus change in value
debt-to-equity ratio, in the model case 225,000 / 84,000 = 2.68
bloecke.erklaerung: Leverage multiplies the difference between the property return and the interest rate; it does not multiply the property return itself. If this difference is negative, every additional dollar of debt increases the loss.

bloecke.titel: Return on equity depending on the equity ratio
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation at an assumed mortgage rate of 7.0%. Leverage amplifies the deviation of the property return from the interest rate, upwards as well as downwards.

bloecke.md:
At 100% equity, each of the two curves equals its property return. Towards the left, that is, with a falling equity ratio, the curves diverge further and further. This effect is called the [[Leverage effect|leverage effect]]. It does not generate any return itself and only amplifies the difference between the property return and the interest rate. At an assumed rate of 7.0%, the threshold is a property return of 7.0%. Expressed in the indicators used in listings, the gross rental yield would have to be around 13.8% with the cost burden assumed here for the leverage to pay for itself from current income. That corresponds to a price-to-rent ratio of about 7. Such properties exist, but rarely in growing metro areas and rarely without deferred maintenance, high crime or problems with tenants.

A financed purchase is therefore not a mistake in every case. Without an increase in value, however, the calculation does not work out at today's rates, and that should be said openly instead of being hidden behind a gross yield.

bloecke.titel: Calculation with a change in value
bloecke.md: If you assume an increase in value of 3% a year, the property return of the model case rises from 4.07% to 7.07%. That is just above the assumed mortgage rate of 7.0%, so leverage now raises the return on equity slightly, to 7.26%. At 2% a year, the property return is 6.07%, still below the rate, and leverage lowers the return on equity to 3.58%. Both figures are assumptions, not forecasts. This argues neither for nor against the purchase. It shows how little buffer a calculation with average values has, and that at today's rates the case rests almost entirely on appreciation.

Two routes raise the current return on equity of the model case from −3.78% to around −1.25%.

With a 10% price discount, the purchase price falls to $270,000, the closing costs to $8,100 and the total investment to $278,100. Property tax and maintenance, which were assumed as a share of the price, fall as well. Net operating income rises to $13,236, the net rental yield to 4.76% and the return on equity, with the same 75% loan, to −1.24%.

With 10% more rent, the rent rises from $2,000 to $2,200, that is, to $26,400 a year. Net operating income is $14,674, the net rental yield 4.75% and the return on equity −1.28%.

Arithmetically, the two routes are almost equivalent; in practice, they are not. The discount takes effect at closing and is certain from then on. The rent increase requires a new lease or a renewal at a higher rent, and the market sets its limit. There is no federal rent control, and many states prohibit local rent control. California and Oregon cap annual increases for many units statewide, and some cities, such as New York City, have rent stabilization for parts of their housing stock. When buying, only the price can be negotiated.

## Effect of vacancy

The 5% vacancy in the model case is an assumption, not a forecast. A single change of tenant can easily cost a month's rent or more through cleaning, repairs, marketing and the search itself. When lenders count rental income to qualify a borrower, Fannie Mae's guidelines generally use only 75% of the gross rent, treating the rest as an allowance for vacancy and maintenance. The debt-to-equity ratio is 2.68 in the model case. Every dollar lost therefore has 3.68 times as strong an effect on the return on equity as on the property return.

bloecke.titel: Vacancy and current return on equity (model case)
Two reasoning errors about the tax side
bloecke.md:
The first error is to regard the loss as an advantage. The tax saving of $2,634 only exists because a loss of $11,975 was incurred. The loss arises because depreciation of $8,873, which costs no cash, is added to a cash shortfall that already exists before depreciation. With a purchase intended mainly to save tax, the buyer spends one dollar to get 22 cents back, and above $150,000 of income, nothing for the time being.

The second error is to regard the saving as permanent or free. The payment remains constant, but the deductible interest portion falls with each payment. With a 30-year loan this happens slowly: in the tenth year, interest is still around $13,700, and with unchanged rent and costs the tax saving falls to around $2,200, while the cash shortfall after tax rises from $2,753 to around $3,200 a year. More importantly, depreciation is largely a deferral. When the property is sold, the depreciation taken is taxed as unrecaptured Section 1250 gain at up to 25%. After ten years, that is $88,727 of depreciation and up to around $22,200 in tax.

bloecke.titel: Depreciation recapture, 1031 exchanges and step-up in basis
bloecke.md:
Three rules decide what happens to the deferred tax. When the property is sold, the gain up to the amount of depreciation allowed is taxed at a maximum rate of 25%, and the remaining gain as a long-term capital gain at 0%, 15% or 20%, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax where it applies. The Section 121 exclusion for a main home does not cover a property that was only rented out.

A like-kind exchange under Section 1031 postpones the tax if the proceeds are reinvested in other real property held for investment or business use. Since 2018, it only applies to real property. The replacement property must be identified within 45 days and acquired within 180 days, and the money must not pass through the seller's hands, which is why a qualified intermediary is used. When the owner dies, the heirs generally receive the property with a basis stepped up to its market value at the date of death (Section 1014), and the deferred tax on depreciation and appreciation is not collected.

These rules show the effect of depreciation and do not compare two investments. Deferral is valuable, but it does not generate any return by itself, and it only becomes permanent if the property is held until death or exchanged again and again.

## Location and demand in twenty years

The return on a rental property depends on two conditions that cannot be bought. In fifteen years' time, someone must still want to live there, and that person must be able to pay the rent. This can be checked using population and employment trends for the county or metro area, the rental vacancy rate, the number of building permits as a measure of future supply and the ratio of rent to local household income. HUD considers households that spend more than 30% of their income on housing to be cost-burdened. Where rents already exceed this share for typical local incomes, further rent increases are limited, regardless of what the market would allow.

Three local factors belong in the assessment as well. Landlord-tenant law differs by state, including how long an eviction takes and how security deposits are handled. Property tax can be reassessed at purchase, and insurance premiums have risen sharply in some regions exposed to hurricanes, wildfires or floods. Both can change the cost side of the calculation more than any interest rate decision.

bloecke.titel: Where high rental yields come from
bloecke.unter: The current yield can only be assessed together with the development of demand.

felder.text: Low price-to-rent ratio in places people are leaving. The yield falls as soon as a change of tenant takes three months, the next tenant pays less and a sale only succeeds below the all-in cost.
A high yield despite growth almost always has a reason: deferred maintenance, a seller under time pressure, difficult tenants or a neighborhood in transition. It rewards work and risk, not capital.
The price level still dates from the low interest rate period, and local rents have not caught up.
Price-to-rent ratio of 20 or more in growing metro areas. The current yield does not cover the financing; everything depends on appreciation and on sustaining the cash shortfalls over the cycle.

bloecke.md:
- Current leases and a rent roll instead of the listing, plus lease start and end dates, the last rent increase and the security deposits held
- Operating statements for the last 12 to 24 months, the current property tax bill and an estimate of the tax after reassessment, and an insurance quote
- Inspection report, receipts for major replacements and building permits on file
- For a condominium or HOA, the rules on renting, which may restrict or prohibit leasing, the budget, the reserve study and any special assessments
- Local requirements such as rental registration, licensing or inspections
- Your own calculation in three variants: expected, with two months' vacancy a year and with insurance and property tax 20% higher

mitnehmen: Gross rental yield, price-to-rent ratio and the 1% rule only serve as sorting criteria; only the cap rate and the net rental yield, based on net operating income, are comparable.

Leverage multiplies the difference between the property return and the mortgage rate; at an assumed 7.0% and the usual cost burden, it only pays for itself from current income below a price-to-rent ratio of about 7.
Principal reallocates wealth and is not income; a rental loss only reduces taxes within the passive activity rules, and depreciation is largely recaptured at up to 25% on sale.
The all-in cost is the only lever that is fully in the buyer's own hands and takes effect immediately, whereas rent increases depend on the market and, in some places, on rent regulation.
Leverage amplifies the effect of vacancy on the return on equity; in the model case, one month of vacancy a year costs around 2.2 percentage points compared with a fully let year.

begriffe.text: Rent actually collected after vacancy, minus property tax, insurance, maintenance, management and HOA dues. Mortgage payments and depreciation are not deducted, so NOI describes the property independently of its financing.
Net operating income divided by the purchase price. It shows the return of the property without financing and before closing costs and changes in value.

Effect of debt financing on the return on equity. Compared with the property return, the return on equity rises by the difference between the property return and the mortgage rate, multiplied by the debt-to-equity ratio. If the difference is negative, it falls accordingly.

Rules in 26 U.S.C. § 469 under which rental losses can normally only offset passive income. Owners who actively participate can deduct up to $25,000 a year from other income; the allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified adjusted gross income.
Taxation of the depreciation taken on a rental building when it is sold. For residential real estate, this part of the gain is taxed as unrecaptured Section 1250 gain at a maximum rate of 25%.
